intro: Munich protects its remarkable trees by law and number: a 2021 city ordinance registers 117 Naturdenkmäler covering 200 trees, each legally protected the way a listed building would be. That bureaucratic precision sits oddly with their origins: planted by a royal count's landscape garden, grown wild in a monastery orchard, set in the ground by twelve thousand schoolchildren celebrating a war's end. Two of the fourteen below carry rival claims to being the city's single oldest tree, and neither is settled. Munich has not tried to force the point.
meta_description: Munich protects 200 trees by city ordinance. Meet a 600-year-old oak, a hollow linden painted by an artist, and eight rare hackberries on a ring road.
question_answer: Munich has no single agreed oldest tree: two different trees carry the claim from different sources. The Krüner Eiche, a pedunculate oak in Sendling-Westpark, is cited by a district citizen assembly as roughly 600 years old, which would date it to the 1420s. The Röth-Linde in Moosach, a winter linden, is separately described by local press as the city's oldest tree at 300 to 350 years. The two claims have never been reconciled against each other.
question_meta: Munich has two rival claims to its oldest tree, a 600-year-old oak and a 300-plus-year-old linden. Both, and thirteen more protected trees, explained.
question_context: Munich's own tally is the most precise starting point any city on this list has offered: a 2021 ordinance names 117 protected Naturdenkmäler covering 200 individual trees across the city, each with a case made for rarity, size, beauty or historical association. Age is a different matter. Ring counts require felling a tree, so every age here comes from growth models, historical association or simple local reputation, not a verified count. The Krüner Eiche's roughly 600-year figure comes from a 2017 Sendling-Westpark district citizen assembly document arguing for the oak's preservation; the Röth-Linde's 300 to 350 year figure, and its billing as Munich's oldest tree, comes from a dedicated local news feature and the tree's own German Wikipedia page. Both are treated here as the honest, sourced claims they are rather than resolved into one winner. The Krüner Eiche stands at Krüner Platz in Sendling-Westpark, an eight minute walk from Harras U-Bahn station.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Munich?
faq.a: Two trees claim the title from different sources: the roughly 600-year-old Krüner Eiche oak in Sendling-Westpark, and the 300 to 350-year-old Röth-Linde in Moosach, separately called the city's oldest tree by local press. Neither claim has been checked against the other.

faq.q: How does Munich protect its old and remarkable trees?
faq.a: By city ordinance. A 2021 update to the Naturdenkmalverordnung lists 117 individually protected natural monuments covering 200 trees across Munich, each legally protected for its age, rarity, size or historical association.

faq.q: Where is the best place to see protected trees in Munich?
faq.a: The Englischer Garten holds three trees on this list within a short walk of each other: the oldest known elms in the city, a beech over 300 years old, and a rare fern-leaved beech cultivar, all in the park's southern half near the Chinese Tower.

faq.q: Are Munich's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Yes. All fourteen stand in public parks, squares and streets with no entry fee, though the Nymphenburg palace grounds around one of them charge for the palace interior itself.

trees.name: The Röth-Linde

best_time.label: June and July, when its flowers scent the whole meadow

trees.story: A painter made this tree famous by sitting under it, and the tree has been fighting for its life ever since. Local tradition holds that the linden was planted as a peace tree after the Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, which would put its planting in the mid-17th century, though like most trees on this list its exact age rests on estimate rather than a documented planting record. By the time landscape painter Philipp Röth worked in its shade around the turn of the 20th century, the tree was already reckoned to be some 200 years old, and it now carries his name and a memorial plaque. That long life has come at a cost: a botched fungal treatment in the 1980s left the trunk hollow, and the tree today stands on eight metal crown braces and a branch support, watered and pruned as what one local report calls an intensive-care patient. Winter lindens can live a thousand years under good conditions, which makes the Röth-Linde's current state, still leafing out every spring at 23 metres tall with a trunk over six metres around, as much a story about arboriculture as about age.
trees.access: Free, public land, viewable from outside Gut Nederling
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Nederlinger Straße bus stop or Moosach S-Bahn station
trees.notes: The Thirty Years' War planting date is local tradition, not a documented record; the 300-350 year range comes from the tree's own Wikipedia entry and matches independently, but no source gives a single precise figure. Photo viewed directly: shows a large, mature, dome-shaped linden standing alone on a grassy plot beside a rural-looking building, consistent with the tree's setting near Gut Nederling. Approved. Cross-checked against an OpenStreetMap node (denotation=natural_monument, name=Röth-Linde) within 5m of this entry's own coordinates: independent confirmation the pin is already right.

trees.name: The Krüner Eiche
trees.story: This oak has outlasted the village it once stood outside, the Bavarian duchy that once ruled the land, and most of its own major branches. A 2017 recommendation from the Sendling-Westpark district's citizen assembly, arguing for the tree's protection and continued care, dates it at roughly 600 years old, which would put its origins in the 1420s, a period when Munich was still ruled directly by Wittelsbach dukes and when Duke Albrecht III married in the city in 1436. No source directly connects the tree's planting to that or any specific historical event, so any such link stays unclaimed here. What is documented is more recent damage: three major limbs have been removed over the years and a fourth broke off on its own, thinning a crown that once spread wide with the snake-like, twisting branch pattern typical of very old pedunculate oaks. A new protective fence went up around the trunk in July 2022 to keep the compacted soil at the roots from getting worse. The tree still stands at the eastern corner of the small park that carries its name, a six-century survivor now fenced off from the joggers and dog walkers who pass it daily.
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Harras U-Bahn station (U3, U6)
trees.notes: The approximately 600-year age comes from a district citizen-assembly document rather than a dendrological survey; baumkunde.de independently suggests a planting date around 1440, consistent with but not identical to that figure. Any connection to Duke Albrecht III's 1436 wedding is local speculation found in searches but not confirmed by either source, so it is not stated as fact in the story. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.4km: German Wikipedia's own list of Munich's Naturdenkmäler (already a cited source) carries per-tree coordinates; independently geocoded 'Krüner Platz' via Nominatim to cross-check rather than trust the table blindly, and it lands within about 100m of the table's figure, confirming the table over the previous stored point, which was the actual error. Photo found and approved 2026-07-28: file titled "Stieleiche (Naturdenkmal) in Sendling-Westpark", an exact species and district match. Viewed directly: a massive old oak with a heavily gnarled, twisting branch structure and thick low limbs behind a garden fence, consistent with the story's description of storm-thinned limbs and the July 2022 protective fence.

trees.name: The Reichs- und Friedenseiche
trees.story: Twelve thousand schoolchildren planted this oak in one afternoon, or at least watched a handful of their classmates do it. On 1 July 1871, weeks after the peace treaty ending the Franco-Prussian War was signed in Frankfurt, Munich staged a peace festival at the Flaucher meadows along the Isar: a procession of children, city councillors and guests gathered while selected boys and girls set a young oak sapling into the ground. A plaque at the site still reads, in German, Reich and Peace Oak, planted by the youth of the city of Munich on 1 July 1871, making this one of the few trees on this list with an exact, undisputed planting date rather than an estimate. Similar Friedenseichen went into the ground across German cities that year, each one a small piece of civic theatre marking the unification of the German Empire under Kaiser Wilhelm I as much as the peace itself. This one has had a century and a half since to grow into an ordinary, unremarkable-looking oak in a riverside park, its real distinction lying entirely in the date rather than the trunk.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Brudermühlbrücke tram/bus stop
trees.notes: Planting date (1 July 1871) is explicit on the tree's own plaque per stadtgeschichte-muenchen.de, so age is calculated directly rather than estimated. Photo viewed directly: shows a large solitary oak on a park lawn with a memorial stone at its base, consistent with a commemorative planting. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.3km, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table against an independent Nominatim geocode).

trees.name: The Beech of the Englischer Garten

best_time.label: late October, when its leaves turn copper, older than the park Count Rumford built around it

location.address: Englischer Garten, near Forstweg, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: This beech was already old when the park around it was new. The Englischer Garten was laid out from 1789 on the orders of Elector Karl Theodor, designed by the American-born Sir Benjamin Thompson, Count Rumford, as one of the first public parks on the European continent, open to everyone rather than reserved for a court. Most of what grows in the park today dates from that design and its later 19th century expansion, but this beech, standing between the Forstweg and Friedrich-Ludwig-von-Sckell-Weg paths near the park's second riding trail, predates the whole project, described in Munich's own natural monument register as over 300 years old and the outstanding tree of its immediate surroundings. That would put its origins in the very early 18th century or before, decades ahead of Rumford's landscaping crews, meaning the park's designers either built around an existing tree or the beech simply outgrew whatever else stood nearby before them. No individual measurement or precise felling-based age exists for it, so the three-century figure is treated here as the registered estimate it is rather than a settled fact.
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Universität U-Bahn station, or bus to Nationalmuseum/Haus der Kunst
trees.notes: Age given only as 'over 300 years' in the city's own Naturdenkmal register (via baumkunde.de and the Wikipedia list drawing on it); no more precise figure or measurement found. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.6km, using that same Wikipedia list's per-tree coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table). Photo found and approved 2026-07-28: file titled "Naturdenkmal Rotbuche Englischer Garten München", the photographer's own title naming this as the specific protected specimen rather than any beech in the park. Viewed directly: a single tall, mature beech standing alone in an open grass clearing, bare in winter, consistent with the Englischer Garten's open meadow sections.

trees.name: The Twin Elms of the Englischer Garten
trees.age_estimate: undated, described as the oldest elms in the city

location.address: Englischer Garten, near the Chinese Tower, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: Munich's own natural monument register makes a specific, checkable claim about these two trees: no older elms are known anywhere in the city. Standing northwest of the Monopteros temple and southwest of the Chinese Tower, in the busiest part of the Englischer Garten, the pair are European white elms, a species that has fared better against Dutch elm disease than most of its European relatives but is still uncommon at real size in any German city after the epidemic spread through the 20th century. Neither tree carries an individual measured age, so the claim rests on comparison rather than a number, but it is specific and official rather than a vague tourist superlative, made by the same city ordinance that protects 200 trees across Munich by name. Thousands of visitors pass within metres of the two elms every week on their way to the Chinese Tower's beer garden, most without knowing they are walking past the oldest confirmed elms the city can point to.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Chinesischer Turm bus stop or Universität U-Bahn station
trees.notes: 'No older elms known in the city area' is the register's own wording, a comparative claim rather than an absolute age; no individual figure exists for either tree. Photo viewed directly: shows a tall, mature tree with a complex, high-branching crown rising above the surrounding autumn canopy in a park setting, consistent with the paired elms. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.5km: German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list gives this exact coordinate, and independently, the approved photo's own file description places the trees 'in der Weggabelung etwa 200m nordwestlich des Monopteros' (at the path fork about 200m northwest of the Monopteros); geocoding the Monopteros directly and projecting 200m northwest lands within about 70m of the Wikipedia table's point, a genuine independent cross-check rather than trusting one source alone.

trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech

best_time.label: October, when its narrow, feathery leaves turn golden bronze

location.address: Englischer Garten, west bank of the Schwabinger Bach near the Chinese Tower, Schwabing-Freimann, 80802 München

trees.story: Most of the Englischer Garten's protected trees are old because they survived. This one is protected because it barely exists anywhere else in Munich. The fern-leaved beech is a naturally occurring form of the common European beech in which the leaves grow narrow, deeply cut and lace-like instead of the usual broad oval, a genetic quirk that occasionally turns up in beech forests and gets propagated deliberately when someone notices it. Munich's specimen, standing west of the administrative building near the Chinese Tower on the bank of the Schwabinger Bach stream, has a trunk 3.67 metres around and is registered by the city specifically for how rare the form is within Munich rather than for size or documented age, unlike most of the natural monuments on this list. From a distance in full leaf it can look almost feathery compared to an ordinary beech standing nearby, a small, deliberate anomaly kept alive in one of the park's quieter corners rather than along its main paths.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Chinesischer Turm bus stop
trees.notes: Protected for rarity of form rather than age; no source gives a planting date or age estimate, so the age range here is a rough guess based on trunk girth rather than a documented figure, flagged accordingly. Photo viewed directly: shows a large dome-shaped beech with a finely textured autumn canopy in a park setting with benches beneath it, consistent with a protected specimen beech. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 1.4km, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_005 for the independent Monopteros cross-check that validated this same table for its immediate neighbour).

trees.name: The Oak of the Dörfchen, Nymphenburg
trees.age_estimate: undated, called unique in size for the city

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, near the Brunnhaus, 80638 München

trees.story: This oak grows in the one part of a royal palace garden built to look like it wasn't designed at all. The Dörfchen, or little village, is a cluster of rustic farm-style buildings inside Nymphenburg Palace Park, built from 1803 as a picturesque contrast to the palace's formal Baroque and later English-landscape grounds surrounding it, complete with a working dairy and a chapel meant to evoke ordinary rural life for an audience that never had to live it. The oak stands near the Brunnhaus, on the way toward the Badenburg pavilion and the park's Großer See lake, and Munich's own natural monument register singles it out as unique in size within the city, a claim about scale rather than age, since no source gives the tree a documented planting date or precise age. What is certain is that it has grown large enough, inside grounds that have been continuously maintained by the Bavarian royal family and its successors since the 17th century, to earn individual legal protection in a park already full of centuries-old formal avenues.
trees.access: Free, public park (the palace interior and botanical garden charge separate admission)
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Schloss Nymphenburg tram stop (line 17)
trees.notes: No source gives this specific oak a documented age; 'unique in size within the city area' is the register's own claim about scale, not age, and is presented as such. Photo found via the city's own Naturdenkmal list, whose Commons category and filename explicitly name this exact tree. Viewed directly: shows a tall, thick-trunked oak with a gnarled, moss-covered lower crown, budding in early spring, next to a rustic tiled-roof building, consistent with the Dörfchen's farm-style setting. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 550m, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table).

trees.name: The Hackberries of Oskar-von-Miller-Ring
trees.age_estimate: undated, described as an extremely rare species group in the city

location.address: Oskar-von-Miller-Ring, near the Siemens headquarters, Maxvorstadt, 80333 München

trees.story: Eight Mediterranean trees grow on a green strip beside one of Munich's busiest ring roads, in a city more than 500 kilometres north of where the species grows wild. Celtis australis, native across southern Europe and North Africa, is registered by Munich as an extremely rare species within the city area, and this group of eight, standing on a green strip on Oskar-von-Miller-Ring west of the Siemens corporate headquarters, is protected as a natural monument specifically for that rarity rather than for any individual tree's size or age. No source gives the group a planting date, though a stand of eight mature specimens growing together suggests a single deliberate planting rather than volunteers that seeded themselves over time, most likely as an ornamental choice for the street rather than a remnant of anything older. Traffic on the ring road runs past them constantly, an odd setting for what the city's own records treat as a genuine botanical rarity worth the same legal protection as its oldest oaks and lindens.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Karlsplatz (Stachus) or Königsplatz U-Bahn stations
trees.notes: Presented as an ensemble of eight trees per the city's own register entry; no individual age or planting date documented for any of the eight. Photo found via the city's own Naturdenkmal list, whose Commons category and filename explicitly name this exact group. Viewed directly: shows a dense cluster of mature trees on a grass strip beside a road, with a Siemens-branded office building behind them, matching the story's own description exactly. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 415m, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table).

trees.name: The Japanese Pagoda Tree of Karolinenplatz
trees.age_estimate: undated, protected for rarity of size in the cityscape

best_time.label: August, the quietest month of the year for almost anything else blooming in Munich

trees.story: This tree flowers in August, the quietest month of the year for almost anything else blooming in Munich, and does it well enough into old age that the city has singled it out for legal protection twice over, once for rarity of species and once for its unusual size. Styphnolobium japonicum, despite the common name, is native to China rather than Japan and was introduced to European gardens in the 18th century for exactly this trait: heat tolerance, resistance to drought and pollution, and a late, generous flowering of small cream-white blooms that pollinators rely on after most spring flowerers are finished. Munich's specimen stands on the grounds of the property at Karolinenplatz 2a, part of a formal obelisk square laid out in the early 19th century to commemorate Bavarian soldiers who died in Napoleon's Russian campaign, a considerably more sober origin than the tree growing on it. No source gives the tree a documented planting date, but the city's own register notes its size is rare for the species within Munich's built-up centre, an urban tree doing more than its share of feeding late-summer bees.
trees.access: Free, viewable from the public square and street
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Königsplatz U-Bahn station
trees.notes: Attribution resolved by checking the file's own description page directly: Martinus KE, CC BY-SA 4.0. Photo viewed directly: shows a large tree with fine, compound pinnate foliage (consistent with Sophora japonica) beside a residential building near the square. Approved. Pin corrected 2026-07-27, about 280m, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table).

trees.name: The Wych Elm of Maximiliansplatz
trees.age_estimate: undated, large specimens rare in the city due to Dutch elm disease
trees.story: Almost every elm this size that once grew in Munich is gone, and that absence is the entire reason this one is protected. Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by bark beetles, swept through European elm populations across the 20th century in repeated waves, and Munich's own natural monument register notes plainly that wych elms of any real size have become rare across the whole city as a result, inner districts included. This one has survived on Maximiliansplatz, a roughly 300 by 60 metre park-like square laid out in the English-garden style along what was once the city's western fortification line, redesigned into a green public space after the walls came down in the 19th century. No source gives the tree an individual planting date or precise age, and its story here is less about a specific event than about what elm disease has quietly removed from cities across the continent: a species that was once an unremarkable street and park tree is now something Munich has to name and legally protect just to keep a mature specimen standing.
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Odeonsplatz or Lenbachplatz
trees.notes: No individual age or planting date documented; rarity is explicitly tied to Dutch elm disease losses across the city rather than this tree's own age. Photo viewed directly: shows a tall mature tree in a city square with buildings visible behind the canopy, consistent with a Maximiliansplatz specimen. Approved. Pin tightened 2026-07-27, about 85m, using German Wikipedia's Naturdenkmäler list coordinates (see muc_002 for the cross-check that validated this table).

trees.name: The Copper Beech of the Badenburg
trees.age_estimate: undated, protected for its size and its setting beside the Badenburg

best_time.label: late April and May, when the new leaves open translucent red before darkening

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, about 25 m south of the Badenburg, 80638 München

trees.story: Every copper beech in Europe descends from an accident. The purple leaf is a mutation that appears rarely and at random in wild green beech forests, and every ornamental one since has been propagated by gardeners who found the freak worth keeping. This one stands about 25 metres south of the Badenburg, the bathing pavilion Joseph Effner built for Elector Max Emanuel between 1718 and 1721 around what is generally reckoned the first heated indoor pool built in Europe since Roman times. Munich's natural monument ordinance protects the tree as a solitary specimen and gives its relationship with that building as the reason, which is a statute saying out loud that where a tree stands can matter as much as how big it is. Local descriptions of the park rank it among the mightiest beeches anywhere in the city. Its age is not documented anywhere. What is documented is the ground: Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell converted these grounds from a French baroque garden into an English landscape park between 1799 and 1823, which is when most of the park's free-standing specimen trees were placed, so a planting inside that window is plausible without being proven. Come in late April and the new leaves open a bright translucent red, darkening to near black by August.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 20 min walk west through the park
trees.notes: Age undated: Munich's Naturdenkmal ordinance carries no age or girth column, and no second source gives this tree a date, so the 150-250 range is inferred from Sckell's documented 1799-1823 landscape redesign rather than measured. Existence, species, location and protection are legally attested by the 2021 ordinance; ownership is Freistaat Bayern, public parkland. Flagged because the ordinance is effectively the only source on the tree itself. Photo viewed directly at 1280px before approval: daylight, colour, deep blue sky, the dark purple crown unmistakable against the green trees beside it, trunk visible at the base, and the yellow baroque Badenburg in frame at left, which corroborates the register's stated Badenburg connection. Survives a wide card crop; the tree holds the centre band.

trees.name: The Leaning Lime of the Badenburger See
trees.age_estimate: undated in the city register; a tree-recorders' database estimates roughly 180 years

best_time.label: midwinter, when the leaves drop and the whole leaning frame shows over the ice

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, about 50 m northwest of the Badenburg on the lake shore, 80638 München

trees.story: Munich protects this lime, in law, for being strange looking. The reason recorded in the city's natural monument ordinance is bizarrer und knorriger Wuchs, bizarre and gnarled growth, together with a striking appearance, which is an unusually candid thing for a protection statute to say about a tree. It earns it. The trunk leans hard out over the Badenburger See and the whole crown follows, throwing its heaviest limbs sideways across the water rather than upward, so the tree reads as a single long gesture toward the lake. A bench sits underneath, facing the Monopteros on the far shore. A German tree-recorders' database measured the trunk at 4.2 metres around in 2014 and the height at 19 metres, and estimates the tree at about 180 years, which would place its planting inside Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell's conversion of these grounds into an English landscape park between 1799 and 1823. That figure is a volunteer estimate rather than an official one, and the city's own register gives no age at all. Come in winter and the case for the tree is at its clearest: bare, every crooked limb legible against the sky, the lake frozen behind it and the pavilion small and white in the distance.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 20 min walk west through the park
trees.notes: The 180-year figure comes from baumkunde.de register entry 4054, a community-compiled German tree register, used here as a lead and named as such in the story rather than as an authority; the city ordinance carries no age column. Its coordinates (48.15457, 11.49279) fall about 33 m from the ordinance's, which independently corroborates the pin. Flagged because the only numeric age is volunteer-sourced. Photo viewed directly at 1280px before approval and run through the Cadiz test deliberately, since it is a bare winter shot: it is daylight and in colour, not black and white, with blue sky, warm brown far bank and ice on the lake. The tree fills the left and centre of the frame with trunk and full crown readable, a bench at its base for scale and the Badenburg visible across the water. It survives a wide card crop because the trunk and the heavy lateral limbs sit in the centre band. Approved. The bare silhouette best_time is the register's own stated reason for protection, not an invented peak.

trees.name: The Fern-leaved Beech of the Amalienburg
trees.age_estimate: undated in the city register; a tree-recorders' database estimates roughly 180 years

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, at the path fork about 50 m south of the Amalienburg, 80638 München

trees.story: No fern-leaved beech anywhere is much more than two centuries old, because the tree did not exist before about 1804. It is a cultivated form of the ordinary European beech whose leaves are cut into narrow ribbons, and it cannot be relied on to come true from seed, so every one of them has been grafted or struck from cuttings taken off another. That gives this specimen an unusually hard ceiling on its age, which is useful in a park where almost nothing else has a date. It stands alone at a fork in the path about 50 metres south of the Amalienburg, the rococo hunting lodge Francois de Cuvillies built in the 1730s, with a small metal plate on the trunk marking it as a natural monument. Munich's ordinance calls it a mighty and rare solitary specimen in a good position, and a German tree-recorders' database measured it in 2019 at 2.95 metres around and 25 metres tall, estimating roughly 180 years and recording its condition as vital. Look closely at the foliage and the trick of the tree becomes clear: most of the leaves are shredded to threads, but a branch here and there reverts and throws out ordinary broad beech leaves instead.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 10 min walk west through the park
trees.notes: Named 'of the Amalienburg' deliberately: muc_006 is already 'The Fern-leaved Beech', in the Englischer Garten, and two entries cannot share a name. Same species, different tree, roughly 7 km apart. The 180-year figure and the vitality note come from baumkunde.de register entry 4055, a community-compiled German register, used as a lead and attributed in the story rather than treated as authority; the city ordinance carries no age column. Its coordinates (48.15538, 11.50030) fall about 15 m from the ordinance's, independently corroborating the pin, and its 2019 condition note is the only vitality evidence available for any tree in this cluster. Photo viewed directly at 1280px before approval: daylight, colour, the tree fills the frame with the smooth silvery trunk running the full height and the finely cut foliage readable, path and boulders at the base for scale. Survives a wide card crop, trunk squarely in the centre band. Approved.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Schwanenbrücke

location.address: Schlosspark Nymphenburg, south of the Schwanenbrücke, 80638 München

trees.story: Munich protects this beech partly because people are fond of it. The reason entered in the city's natural monument ordinance is that it is a dominant tree in a historic garden with besondere Bedeutung für Münchner Bürger, particular significance for the citizens of Munich, which is a legal document recording public affection as grounds for protection. That is rarer than it sounds; most entries on the same list argue from size, rarity or townscape effect. The tree stands just south of the Schwanenbrücke, the swan bridge over the canal that runs north through the park. A weeping beech grows nothing like the wild form it was bred from: instead of a clean grey column carrying a high crown, the limbs arch outward and then fall, so the branches hang to the ground and the whole tree closes around a hollow space at its centre. Walking under one is the point of it, and generations of Munich children have done exactly that here. Its age is not recorded anywhere. The cultivar has only been in general garden circulation since the early nineteenth century, and the surrounding park was landscaped between 1799 and 1823, which brackets it loosely and honestly without pretending to a date.
trees.access: Free, public park, open daily (the palace, Amalienburg and Badenburg interiors charge separate admission)
trees.transport: Tram 17 to Schloss Nymphenburg, then about 15 min walk northwest through the park
trees.notes: Age undated and no second source beyond the ordinance itself, so flagged. The 120-200 range is bracketed from the cultivar's introduction date and Sckell's 1799-1823 landscaping, not measured; baumkunde.de has no entry for this tree. Photo deliberately left missing rather than filled. Three candidates exist on Wikimedia Commons and all three were checked: the register-linked 'Haengebuche im Schlosspark Nymphenburg.jpg' was viewed directly at 1280px and fails the Cadiz standard, being a close-up shot looking up into the canopy with no trunk base, no whole-tree shape and no sense of scale, plus a painted red heart on one limb; the other two ('Unter der Haengebuche', 'Laub der Haengebuche') are by the same photographer and are respectively an under-canopy and a foliage close-up, failing the same way. An honest gap beats a mediocre photo. Worth re-hunting when someone photographs this tree whole.
